Over the years, I've discovered that I have personal boundaries that are both predictably stereotypical, and some that are just weird (at least, I perceive them as weird.

On the predictable side, I absolutely dislike being touched-- at all. It sounds like a horrible stereotypical cliche, I know.

Of the weirder personal boundaries, one is that I feel extremely uncomfortable entering another person's bedroom without being explicitly invited. It doesn't matter who's bedroom it is. I recall once I was helping my buddy move, and we had to pack up his bed frame. He went in, and I stopped at the door until he said I could come in. An ex even once poked fun at me about it. We'd been dating exclusively for more than a year and lived in different apartments. She was surprised that I would always wait at the door until she explicitly invited me into her bedroom.

Oddly, I'm less restrictive with my own bedroom, but still have some firm boundaries. I don't mind if people I know very well walk in and out of it all day long. But if I've only known you for a couple of months, or you're a rando or acquaintance attending one of the parties I (used to) throw, stay the fuck out unless I explicitly tell you it's okay. Strangely, the "don't come into my room unless I tell you to" boundary with strangers extends to animals, despite the fact that I'm very much an animal person.

Another weird boundary I have is food and drinks. I've gotten ridiculously enraged when someone just takes food from my plate without asking. Yet, I've also never turned anyone down who has asked. If you ask, I'll always share. If you take so much as a french-fry without asking, you're liable to have your hand stabbed by a fork.

Beverages are basically the same, but go a step further. I have a difficult time drinking from the same cup/glass/etc as someone else. I've even poured a sip's worth into another glass either for me (if the drink is someone else's) or them (if the drink is mine). But that's not the weird part. The weird part is that this boundary changes if the owner of the drink is done with it. That is to say, if someone's had enough of their cola and hands me their half-full glass, then I have no problem drinking from that glass (and vice versa).

Weird, right?

Nero arrived with a large and colorful entourage in Greece in the early autumn of the year AD 66, ready to participate in all the major Greek contests. To do this, even though the different games were normally celebrated in different years, he ordered that they all be held within the year of his visit. Some of them then had to be given twice, but the Olympics whose celebration had been due in the year 65, were actually postponed for the first time in more than eight centuries, until his arrival in the following year.

Nero, who desperately wanted the glory to be won in these most traditional of competitions, was nevertheless determined to recreate the tradition on his own terms. Not only were the games of the 211th Olympiad delayed for a year, they were also pushed back from summer to autumn. To the athletic contests were added for the first time artistic competitions, which included singing and acting, for Nero's sake. In the area near the gymnasium where visitors to the games had pitched their tents for centuries, Nero erected an elaborate pavilion, tent-like but permanent, while near the great sanctuary of Zeus he built a luxurious palaestra in which to train.

In one dangerous race he fell out of his chariot, but the Hellenistic Judges in charge of the games nevertheless granted him the wreath of victory; he rewarded these traditionally unpaid officials with one million sesterces. Without a doubt, the emperor won every contest in which he competed.

After his death the Games reverted to their normal cycle, with the 212th Olympiad beginning on schedule in 69, but Nero's bold experiment left a permanent blemish: for chronographical reasons the 211th Olympiad could not be omitted, but the official Olympiad records at Elis passed over its games and their winners in silence.

Source:

Champlin, Edward. "Portrait of the Artist." Nero. Cambridge, Mass.: Belknap of Harvard UP, 2003. 54. Print.
